rv.q: This is a bold, clear, finally harrowing account of the play.
Adark, devastating, triumphant Hedda for our times.

Van Hove may overdo the Brack-is-to-blame perspective, but his stripped-down approach, with a baseline of near-screen naturalism until particular intensity is required, works beautifully at reinvigorating Ibsen.
Wilson’s fine Hedda possesses a mad spirit lurking inside the body of a social conservative.
Ruth Wilson brings a thrilling volatility to its title role.
The star, the reason to go, is Wilson who plays Hedda with a cool and sneery nonchalance that at times slips almost into a trance.
Ruth Wilson has brought a new dimension to Hedda Gabler.
There is an almost hypnotic rhythm to the delivery, though there are times when this leads to the dialogue feeling cold and clinical.
But although it all starts in a blaze of modishness and has you thinking ‘director Ivo van Hove has done it again’, in the second half the drama slowly collapses as a credible proposition.

Ivo van Hove’s HEDDA GABLER at the National Theatre is an unforgettable production that will hopefully be seen by many young theatre makers inspiring them to create bold and radical work and changing the way so many perceive Ibsen’s work.
This is not an act of historical reconstruction but a radical rethinking so gripping that you find yourself leaning in, listening to nuance, wondering what exactly happens next.
Ruth Wilson towers over this performance, joining the lengthy ranks of female performers who have excelled in 2016.

Why doesn't Hedda Gabler make more of herself? His is a clinical evaluation of a difficult play. Though it brings the action into the present, this isn't just an update of Ibsen, or one that finds Hedda as she exists in our world.
Patrick Marber’s script reinvigorates Ibsen’s fine play and is a model of clarity, laced with lethal nuance.

cn.t: Ruth Wilson delivers a compelling, incandescent performance in van Hove's stark, minimalist production, though critics are divided on the austere staging. Most praise Wilson's portrayal of Hedda's toxic despair and volatility.
